new_statements.quote: Aussagen zum Akzent im Alur finden wir ausschließlich in Knappert (1963: 70). Dieser schreibt, daß Wurzelmorpheme den Wortakzent tragen. Hat das Wurzelmorphem die Struktur KVKV, dann liegt der Akzent auf dem ersten Vokal. In Wörtern mit der Struktur VKVKV wird der zentrale Vokal akzentuiert. [...] habe ich die Frage der Artikulation und Positionierung des Wortakzents im Alur mit einem Muttersprachler überprüft. Dabei konnte festgestellt werden, daß der Akzent durch die Erhöhung des Lungendrucks bei gleichzeitiger Längung des ihn tragenden Segments ausgedrückt wird. Die Rolle des Wurzelvokals als Akzentträger konnte mit den folgenden Beispielen bestätigt werden: /'camo/ to [eat] ...
new_statements.translation: Statements on accent in Alur are found only in Knappert (1963: 70). He writes that root morphemes carry the word accent. If the root morpheme has the structure CVCV, the accent lies on the first vowel. In words with the structure VCVCV the central vowel is accented. [...] I checked the question of the articulation and positioning of the word accent in Alur with a native speaker. It was established that the accent is expressed by an increase of lung pressure with simultaneous lengthening of the segment that bears it. The role of the root vowel as accent bearer was confirmed with the following examples: /'camo/ to [eat] ... (Heusing 2006, p. 73f., in English: 'In examples 1-4 it is always the root vowel which carries the stress no matter whether pre- and/or suffixes are added to the root. And in example 5, which is a noun based on a disyllabic root, it is the first root vowel which carries the stress.')
new_statements.citation: Heusing, Gerald. 2004. Die südlichen Lwoo-Sprachen: Beschreibung, Vergleich und Rekonstruktion. (Nilo-Saharan: Linguistic Analyses and Documentation 19.) Köln: Rüdiger Köppe. XVIII+383 pp. ISBN 978-3-89645-137-8.
new_statements.locator: §3.1.2.3 'Alur', p. 161 (page confirmed by the DNB table-of-contents scan and the '161' page footer inside the snippet); general statement §3.1 'Wortakzent', p. 157; corroborated in English by Heusing 2006, 'Loanwords in Alur (Western Nilotic)', Tables 10-11, pp. 73-74
new_statements.rule_in_words: Alur is a tone language (two levels H/L per Heusing; Knappert 1969 counts H, M, L) with a non-distinctive, bound dynamic word accent that sits on the root morpheme: the (first) root vowel carries it regardless of prefixes or suffixes (/'cam-o/ 'to eat', /ê-'cám-é/ 'he eats it', /'gak-írí/ 'to avoid each other', /'dhógól-á/ 'door'); CVCV roots accent the first vowel, VCVCV words the central vowel. Loanwords keep the stress position of the donor language (/sù'kúru/ 'school', /daki'tár/ 'doctor', /senthì'méthrì/ 'centimetre'). Knappert 1969 describes the same root prominence as vowel lengthening and says intensity stress is 'not significant'; Heusing's native-speaker check found raised pulmonary pressure plus lengthening.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any snippet examined.
new_statements.exceptions: Reduplicated roots: no syllable especially prominent, or exceptionally the first syllable (/'momo/ 'oily' < /'mò/ 'oil'); in the reconstruction section Heusing states that in Alur, Adhola and Luo the accent of reduplicated forms falls on the first vowel (the vowel of the reduplicated part), against Acholi/Kumam/Lango (second vowel). Loanwords retain donor-language stress (English, Swahili; a Swahili penultimate-stress form is used to argue direct borrowing from Swahili rather than Arabic) and usually carry a falling tone on the syllable stressed in the source language (Heusing 2004 §3.2, data from Ukoko/Knappert/Spaandonck 1964).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (root morpheme + affixes) in cognate vocabulary and in loanwords; accent has no distinctive/grammatical function but conditions tone sandhi (Heusing 2004: 157; Storch 2005 §4.3). Heusing's synchronic data are from Western (Congo) Alur samples and one native-speaker consultant; Knappert's data are Congo (Mahagi) Dho-Alur. Access caveat: all quotations are verbatim scanned fragments returned by the public Google Books feed for books without page preview, saved to disk; the full text has not been read.
new_statements.identity_note: Sources describe Alur proper (alur1250 / alz). Heusing 2004 separates West-Alur (DR Congo, Mahagi side) and Ost-Alur (Uganda) for some consonant features; Storch notes his samples are Western Alur, and his native-speaker accent check does not name the dialect. Knappert 1962/1963/1969 and the 1964 Ghent dictionary describe Congo (Mahagi) Dho-Alur; Ringe 1953 is Ugandan Alur. No separate glottocode for these dialects (Jonam, Jokot, Mambisa, Wanyoro are listed as subdialects on Wikipedia).

sources.note: Second-hand for Alur: 'Stress may be present in many Western Nilotic languages, but exclusively has been attested to have lexical and grammatical functions in Dinka and Shilluk... Heusing (2002: 143) notes that stress (Wortakzent) is present in Southern Lwoo, where it may be reconstructed for the Proto-language level. This phenomenon has no grammatical functions in Southern Lwoo, but plays a role in the context of tone sandhi. The tonal systems of Southern Lwoo are insofar exceptional within Western Nilotic, as they distinguish between only two levels'; 'Burun and Southern Lwoo are exceptions…
